task: Predict whether a module of NASA flight software for an earth-orbiting satellite has reported defects.
instructions: You are helping a feature-selection search for a classification task. Rate how useful each feature is likely to be for predicting the class, on its own or together with a few others, from 0 (useless) to 1 (most useful). Use only your knowledge of the domain and the descriptions given; you do not see the data. Reply with a JSON object only: {"scores": {"<feature index>": <score>, ...}} with one entry for every feature index listed.

calls.reply:
The feature names are hidden, so I scored by guessing which NASA MDP metrics sit at each index. The 37-feature set looks like a PC-style dataset (for example PC1 or PC3, or a similar one), and I assumed an ordering I could not verify.

The assumed order is: loc, v(g), ev(g), iv(g), n, v, l, d, i, e, b, t, lOCode, lOComment, lOBlank, lOCodeAndComment, uniq_Op, uniq_Opnd, total_Op, total_Opnd, branchCount, and so on. Newer versions have extra features such as the McCabe densities, node and edge counts, and decision counts.

Because the ordering is a guess, I kept the scores moderate and spread them out. In the usual software-defect literature, size and complexity metrics are the most predictive: LOC, Halstead volume and effort, cyclomatic complexity, branch count, and total operators and operands. Comment and blank-line counts are weaker. Density and ratio features tend to be noisier.

I gave higher scores to the early indices, which probably hold the size and complexity metrics, and to the middle indices, which probably hold the Halstead metrics. The later indices are probably densities and counts, so they got lower scores.
